lines.text: the coming One. But inasmuch as Advent proclaims not
only His ever expected future coming, to which we look
forward in every distress and sore temptation, but proclaims
also His having come in the Holy Nativity, it draws our
attention at the same time to that unique miracle which
summons us to decision. For the Holy Nativity of our Saviour
is a miracle in the twofold sense that at this point there is
proclaimed loud and clear to the poor the good news of the
eternal light which transforms the appearance of the world,
and also in that through this Word the flame of divine love
is once more kindled among us.
For the Incarnation is a sheer miracle. The feast of
Christmas which celebrates it has as a result lost just that
sense which in pagan times characterized the festival of the
winter solstice. The Christian feast is precisely not a festival
growing out of the regular rhythm of nature and human lite
which is so closely intertwined with nature. Rather as a
Christian feast it is torn out of nature's continuity and
becomes the celebration of the miracle that to the poor
of this world the good news is preached. No doubt this
Christian feast is so deeply rooted in our whole way of life
that it is also accompanied by much natural love and
kindness which is not awakened by the Word. So much the
more, for us Christians, this Word of the Gospel should stand
right at the heart of the feast, penetrating, deepening and
limiting all natural love, so that our love, awakened by the
Word, should take on the quality of a witness to that Word.
Whether we are truly preparing ourselves to receive with
expectant hearts the One who is to come, we can decide as
we ponder seriously the lines of the old Advent hymn:
"And he who would embrace and kiss the Holy Child with
joy
In pain and torment with Him first his spirit must employ.
Thereafter die as He has died, with Him to rise and reign;
For he who treads the Saviour's path, His deathless life
shall gain."
